concepts.name: The cornea and lens act as one thin lens that forms a real, inverted image on the retina
concepts.why: Everything the chapter says about vision rests on this model. Once the eye is treated as a single converging lens a fixed distance from a screen, the thin lens equations of the last chapter describe it completely, and every defect and every correction becomes a question about that one lens.
concepts.evidence: The book states that the cornea and lens form a system that, to a good approximation, acts as a single thin lens, and that for clear vision a real image must be projected onto the light-sensitive retina, which lies at a fixed distance from the lens. It adds that the image is a case 1 image, inverted, and that the brain inverts it once more.

concepts.name: The cornea, not the lens, supplies about two-thirds of the power of the eye
concepts.why: It is natural to suppose that the part called the lens does most of the focusing, and it does not. The largest change in refractive index, and so the greatest bending, is where light passes from air into the cornea, and this is why reshaping the cornea corrects vision.
concepts.evidence: The book says that the biggest change in the refractive index, and bending of rays, occurs at the cornea rather than the lens, and that the cornea provides about two-thirds of the power of the eye, owing to the fact that the speed of light changes considerably while traveling from air into the cornea. Table 26.1 lists the indices.

concepts.name: Accommodation, the eye adjusting its power to keep the image on the retina
concepts.why: Because the retina cannot move, the image distance is fixed, and the only way to focus on objects at different distances is to change the power of the lens. This is the one adjustable part of the eye, and it explains near vision, distant vision and what age does to both.
concepts.evidence: The book states that the image distance must be the same for objects at all distances and that the eye manages this by varying the power and focal length of the lens, a process called accommodation. For close vision the lens is made thicker and more powerful by the ciliary muscle; distant vision is totally relaxed and the closest vision fully accommodated.

concepts.name: The thin lens equations for the eye, $P = 1/\kdobj + 1/\kdimg$ and $\khimg/\khobj = -\kdimg/\kdobj = m$
concepts.why: Writing the thin lens equation in terms of power is what makes the eye quantitative. With the image distance fixed at the lens-to-retina distance, a single number, the power, says what the eye is focused on.
concepts.evidence: The book rewrites the thin lens equations as the power equation and the magnification equation, and notes that the image distance must equal the lens-to-retina distance for clear vision, with normal vision possible from 25 cm to infinity. The section summary states both equations.

concepts.name: Find the power of the eye, or the size of an image on the retina
concepts.why: This is the working skill of the section and the one its problems test. The reader sets the image distance to the lens-to-retina distance, puts every distance in meters, and finds either the power the eye needs or how large an object appears on the retina.
concepts.evidence: Example 26.1 finds the image of a hair at arm's length to be $-4.00 \times 10^{-4}$ cm high, and Example 26.2 finds the power of the eye to range from 50.0 D for distant vision to 54.0 D for close vision, assuming a lens-to-retina distance of 2.00 cm.

concepts.name: Presbyopia, the loss of accommodation with age, corrected by a converging lens
concepts.why: The ability to accommodate shrinks with age, and nearly everyone eventually needs reading glasses. The reader should see that this is a loss of added power for close vision, not a change in distant vision, and that a converging lens supplies the missing power.
concepts.evidence: The book says that an 8% ability to accommodate is typical of people about 40 years old, that the lens changes with age in ways that preserve distant vision but not close vision, a condition called presbyopia, and that it is corrected with a converging, positive power lens such as reading glasses, typically 1.0 to 3.5 D.

concepts.name: Nearsightedness and farsightedness
concepts.why: These are the two most common vision defects, and they are opposites. The reader should be able to say, for each, where the rays from a distant or a close object cross, and whether the eye has too much power or too little.
concepts.evidence: The book states that the nearsighted eye overconverges the nearly parallel rays from a distant object so that they cross in front of the retina, and that the farsighted eye does not converge sufficient rays from a close object to make them meet on the retina. Figure 26.5 shows each caused by a lens of the wrong power or an eye of the wrong length.

concepts.name: The near point and the far point of the eye
concepts.why: Every prescription begins from these two distances. The far point is the farthest object seen clearly, normally infinity, and the near point the closest, normally 25 cm; a defect moves one of them.
concepts.evidence: The book defines the far point as the distance to the farthest object that can be seen clearly and the near point as the distance to the closest, and says that someone wearing glasses sees images that fall between their near point and their far point.

concepts.name: Find the power of a diverging lens that corrects nearsightedness
concepts.why: The correcting lens does not change the eye; it makes an image of a distant object at the person's far point. Finding its power is a thin lens problem in which the image distance is negative and measured from the spectacle.
concepts.evidence: Example 26.3 finds that a person whose far point is 30.0 cm needs a spectacle lens of $-3.51$ D held 1.50 cm from the eye, taking the image distance as $-28.5$ cm for an object at infinity. The book notes that the negative power indicates a diverging lens.

concepts.name: Find the power of a converging lens that corrects farsightedness
concepts.why: The converging lens makes an image of a close object at the person's near point, farther away than the object itself. The reader must measure both distances from the spectacle and give the image distance its negative sign.
concepts.evidence: Example 26.4 finds that a person whose near point is 1.00 m needs a spectacle lens of 3.24 D to see an object 25.0 cm away, with the image distance $-98.5$ cm and the object distance 23.5 cm from a spectacle held 1.50 cm from the eye.

concepts.name: Astigmatism, an unevenness in the focus of the eye
concepts.why: Not every defect is a matter of too much or too little power. Astigmatism is a difference in power along different axes, which is why it needs a cylindrical correction rather than a spherical one.
concepts.evidence: The book describes astigmatism as an unevenness or asymmetry in the focus of the eye, mostly due to irregularities in the shape of the cornea, and says that a cylindrical correction in a prescription is there to correct it, while corrections for short- or farsightedness are spherical. Figure 26.8 is a chart that detects it.

concepts.name: The power of lenses placed close together is the sum of their powers
concepts.why: This is what lets a contact lens, a tear layer or a reshaped cornea be treated as a simple addition to the eye's power. It is an approximation, and it holds because the lenses are close together.
concepts.evidence: The book states that, to a reasonable approximation, the power of multiple lenses placed close together equals the sum of their powers, so that a spectacle lens of $P = -3.00$ D has the same effect as reducing the power of the eye itself by 3.00 D.

concepts.name: Laser vision correction reshapes the cornea
concepts.why: Because the cornea supplies most of the power of the eye, a small change in its curvature does what a spectacle lens does. The reader should know which way to reshape it for each defect and why ultraviolet laser light is used.
concepts.evidence: The book says that to correct nearsightedness the cornea is flattened to reduce its power and to correct farsightedness its curvature is enhanced, and that LASIK ablates the cornea with bursts of 193 nm ultraviolet light, which is strongly absorbed by corneal tissue, removing a layer about $0.3\;\mu\text{m}$ thick with each burst.

concepts.name: Rods and cones, the two kinds of light receptor in the retina
concepts.why: Color vision begins with the cells that sense light. Rods are sensitive and colorless and serve night and peripheral vision; cones need bright light, give color and fine detail, and crowd the fovea.
concepts.evidence: The book states that rods are more sensitive than cones by a factor of about 1000, are solely responsible for peripheral vision and vision in very dark environments, and do not yield color information, and that cones are most concentrated in the fovea, work best in bright light and are responsible for high resolution vision.

concepts.name: Three types of cones and the simplified theory of color vision
concepts.why: The three kinds of cone, each sensitive to a different range of wavelengths, are why three colors of light can produce the thousands of hues we see. The reader should also see the evidence that the theory is incomplete.
concepts.evidence: The book says that there are three types of cones, each sensitive to different ranges of wavelengths as Figure 26.11 shows, and that the simplified theory holds there are three primary colors corresponding to them. It then notes that there is no unique set of three primary colors and that different combinations can produce the same hue.

concepts.name: The true color of an object is set by what it absorbs and reflects
concepts.why: An object's color is a property of the object, not of the light that happens to fall on it. The reader should be able to predict how a colored object appears under light that is not white.
concepts.evidence: The book defines the true color of an object by its absorptive or reflective characteristics and says that a pure blue object illuminated with pure red light will appear black, because it absorbs all the red light falling on it, while its true color remains blue. Figure 26.12 shows four such cases.

concepts.name: A light source's color is set by the wavelengths it emits
concepts.why: Sources differ in their spectra, from the sharp line of a laser to the broad spectrum of the Sun, and that difference is what we see as the color of the light. It sets up the question color constancy answers.
concepts.evidence: The book states that light sources have colors defined by the wavelengths they produce: a helium-neon laser emits pure red light, the Sun a broad yellowish spectrum, fluorescent lights bluish-white light and incandescent lights reddish-white hues, as the spectra of Figure 26.13 show.

concepts.name: Color constancy and the retinex theory
concepts.why: We see a white tablecloth as white under sunlight and under candlelight, though the light reaching the eye is very different. Explaining this takes more than the three cones: the eye and brain compare an object with its surroundings.
concepts.evidence: The book defines color constancy as the ability of the eye-brain system to perceive the true color of an object under varying lighting, notes that the eye compares adjacent receptors and is very sensitive to edges (Figure 26.14), and describes Land's retinex theory, in which the images of three retinexes are compared.

concepts.name: The compound microscope: the image of the objective is the object of the eyepiece
concepts.why: Every instrument of the chapter is built from this one idea. Each lens is treated in turn, and the image one forms becomes the object for the next; in the microscope the objective forms a large case 1 image, and the eyepiece magnifies it as a case 2 magnifier.
concepts.evidence: The book states that the image formed by the first element becomes the object for the second element, and that in the compound microscope of Figure 26.16 the objective forms a case 1 image that is larger than the object, which the eyepiece, placed closer to it than its focal length, magnifies into a final image that remains inverted.

concepts.name: The overall magnification is the product of the magnifications, $m = m_{\text{o}}m_{\text{e}}$
concepts.why: Since each lens multiplies the height of the image it is given, the magnifications multiply. The rule holds for any chain of thin lenses and mirrors, not only for the microscope.
concepts.evidence: The book states that the overall magnification $m$ is the product of the individual magnifications, $m = m_{\text{o}}m_{\text{e}}$, and that this equation can be generalized for any combination of thin lenses and mirrors that obey the thin lens equations.

concepts.name: Find the image and magnification of a two-lens system
concepts.why: This is the procedure every problem of the section asks for. The reader locates the first image, measures its distance from the second lens to get that lens's object distance, and so finds the final image and the overall magnification.
concepts.evidence: Example 26.5 finds that an object 6.20 mm from a 6.00 mm objective, with a 50.0 mm eyepiece 23.0 cm away, is magnified $-250$ times, the objective giving $-30.0$ and the eyepiece 8.33. The book says the procedure is applicable in any multiple-element system and is only lengthier than for a single lens.

concepts.name: Numerical aperture, $\text{NA} = n \sin\alpha$
concepts.why: Magnification alone does not say how much detail an objective can show. The numerical aperture measures how wide a cone of light the lens gathers, and a wider cone gives a higher resolution.
concepts.evidence: The book gives $\text{NA} = n \sin\alpha$, where $n$ is the refractive index of the medium between the lens and the specimen and $\alpha$ is half the angle of acceptance, and says that as the angle of acceptance increases, more light is gathered from a smaller focal region, giving higher resolution.

concepts.name: The $f$-number, $f/\# = \kffoc/\kD \approx 1/(2\,\text{NA})$
concepts.why: The same light-gathering question arises in a camera, where it is stated as the $f$-number. The reader should see that a smaller $f$-number means a wider aperture and more light, and that it is related to the numerical aperture.
concepts.evidence: The book defines the $f$-number as the ratio of the focal length of the lens to the diameter of the aperture, approximately $1/(2\,\text{NA})$ for a small acceptance angle, and says that a greater $f$-number means less light reaches the image plane, so that $f/16$ usually suits bright sunlight.

concepts.name: Immersion objectives make the numerical aperture larger than 1
concepts.why: Filling the gap between the specimen and the objective with oil or water lets rays that would have been refracted away enter the lens. It is Snell's law at work inside the microscope.
concepts.evidence: The book says that the numerical aperture can be larger than 1.00 if a medium such as oil, glycerine or water is placed between the objective and the cover slip, which minimizes the mismatch in refractive indices and allows more rays to enter the objective, increasing the resolution, as Figure 26.19 shows.

concepts.name: Illumination, and microscopes that use x rays and electrons
concepts.why: A microscope is a whole system, not a pair of lenses. The specimen must be lit, by transmission, scattering or reflection, and microscopes that use x rays or electrons in place of light reach far finer detail with the same focusing physics.
concepts.evidence: The book describes condensers that illuminate the specimen by transmission, scattering or reflection (Figure 26.20), and says that x-ray and electron microscopes provide greater resolution, that the focusing and basic physics are the same, and that magnifications of 50 million times can locate individual atoms.

concepts.name: The image of a very distant object forms at the focal length
concepts.why: A telescope views objects that are, for its lenses, at infinity. The thin lens equation then puts the first image exactly one focal length behind the objective, which fixes where the eyepiece goes.
concepts.evidence: The book shows that with $d_{\text{o}} \approx \infty$ the thin lens equation gives $1/d_{\text{i}} = 1/f_{\text{o}}$, so the first image is at $d_{\text{i}} = f_{\text{o}}$, and states that for any distant object and any lens or mirror, the image is at the focal length.

concepts.name: Angular magnification of a telescope, $M = \theta'/\theta = -\kfobj/\kfeye$
concepts.why: A telescope cannot make a distant object larger than it is; it makes it subtend a larger angle at the eye. The ratio of the two angles depends only on the focal lengths, so the design rule is a long objective and a short eyepiece.
concepts.evidence: The book defines the angular magnification as the ratio of the angle subtended by the telescope image to that subtended by the object viewed with the unaided eye, gives $M = \theta'/\theta = -f_{\text{o}}/f_{\text{e}}$, and says the minus sign indicates the image is inverted and that the greatest magnification comes from a long focal length objective and a short focal length eyepiece.

concepts.name: Telescope arrangements that give an inverted or an upright image
concepts.why: The two-convex-lens telescope inverts the image, which does not matter for stars and matters a great deal on a ship. The reader should know the two ways to turn it upright: Galileo's concave eyepiece, or a third lens that inverts it again.
concepts.evidence: The book says Galileo's convex objective and concave eyepiece produce an upright image (Figure 26.23(a)), that most simple telescopes use two convex lenses and give an inverted image (Figure 26.23(b)), and that a more common arrangement uses a third convex lens to invert the image once again (Figure 26.24).

concepts.name: Telescopes with a concave mirror as the objective
concepts.why: A concave mirror acts like a convex lens, and for a telescope it is the better choice. Mirrors can be made far larger than lenses, gather more light, reach long focal lengths and do not suffer from chromatic aberration.
concepts.evidence: The book says that a telescope can be made with a concave mirror as its objective, since a concave mirror acts like a convex lens (Figure 26.25), that mirrors can be constructed much larger than lenses and gather large amounts of light, and that large, relatively flat mirrors have very long focal lengths, so that great angular magnification is possible.

concepts.name: Telescopes that use radio waves and x rays, and adaptive optics
concepts.why: Telescopes, like microscopes, are not limited to visible light. Radio dishes and grazing-incidence x-ray mirrors extend them across the spectrum, and adaptive optics corrects rapidly changing distortions.
concepts.evidence: The book describes the Australia Telescope Compact Array, which maps the sky with radio waves, and the Chandra X-ray Observatory, whose x rays reflect only at small glancing angles off four pairs of mirrors (Figure 26.26), and defines adaptive optics as a lens or mirror built from many tiny elements that computers deform or tilt.

concepts.name: Chromatic aberration, the dependence of a lens's focus on color
concepts.why: Because the index of refraction depends on wavelength, a single lens brings violet to a focus closer than red. The reader should know why mirrors are free of it and how a doublet of two glasses partly corrects it.
concepts.evidence: The book says that since the index of refraction of lenses depends on color or wavelength, images are produced at different places and with different magnifications for different colors, that violet rays are bent more than red, that mirrors do not have this problem, and that an achromatic doublet of crown and flint glass can dramatically reduce it (Figure 26.28).

concepts.name: Coma and spherical aberration
concepts.why: Even in light of one color, a real lens does not bring every ray to one point. Rays from an off-axis object fail to meet in coma, and rays through the edge of a lens focus closer than rays near its axis in spherical aberration.
concepts.evidence: The book states that when the object is off-center, different parts of a lens do not refract the image to the same point, an aberration called a coma that often gives a pear-shaped image (Figure 26.29), and that in spherical aberration rays from the outer edges of a lens converge closer to the lens than rays near the axis (Figure 26.30).

concepts.name: How aberrations are reduced
concepts.why: Every real optical system is a compromise between brightness and sharpness. The remedies range from stopping down the aperture to shaped surfaces, several elements, graded index lenses and correction of the image by computer.
concepts.evidence: The book says that entrance and exit pupils reduce aberrations but also reduce brightness, that looking through a small hole makes an object sharper, and that aberrations are corrected with specially shaped surfaces, several elements, graded index (GRIN) lenses and advanced computing techniques applied after the image is collected.
